title: Strang's example: David's three options (2 Samuel 24); God decreed what David would choose
source_text: XI. Verbi causa, inquit, tria ista quae Deus permisit Optioni Davidis capite vigesimo quarto libri secundi Samuelis, omnia erant licita, id est, quodvis eorum potuit David licite eligere. Permissio enim horum Dei respectu non solum fuit Physica, sed etiam moralis. Deus permisit ei liberam optionem, ut quodcunque ex tribus mallet, id eligeret, non restrinxit ad unum, itaque non decrevit ut solum unum eligeret: sed praescius futurae electionis Davidis, ejusque habita ratione, recte dici potest simpliciter decrevisse pestem futuram, & septuaginta millia hominum occisum iri. Deus enim decrevit id efficere quod David electurus erat, hoc autem electurum eum Deus praeviderat; ergo hoc idem efficere Deus decrevit. De voluntate Dei circa peccatum lib. 3. cap. 2.
pass_a_gloss: XI. For example, he says, those three things which God permitted to David's Option in the twenty-fourth chapter of the second book of Samuel, were all lawful, that is, David could lawfully choose any one of them. For the permission of these on God's part was not only Physical, but also moral. God permitted him free option, that whichever of the three he preferred, he should choose it, he did not restrict him to one, and so did not decree that he should choose only one: but foreknowing David's future election, and having regard to it, he can rightly be said simply to have decreed that the plague would be, and that seventy thousand men would be slain. For God decreed to effect that which David was going to choose, and God had foreseen that he would choose this; therefore God decreed to effect this same thing. On the will of God concerning sin book 3, chap. 2.
pass_b_english: He offers an example, saying: the three things God left to David's choice in 2 Samuel 24 were all lawful options; David could rightly pick any of them, since God's leave here was moral and not merely physical.

God left him free to take whichever of the three he liked best, did not confine him to one, and so made no decree that he should choose only one. Yet because God knew in advance what David would choose and took that into account, one may rightly say that God simply decreed that pestilence should come and that seventy thousand men should be killed.

God decreed to carry out whatever David would choose; he had foreseen that David would choose this; so it was this that God decreed to carry out. (Strang, On the Will of God concerning Sin, book 3, chapter 2.)
